utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. All accused are here. Defence teams are all here, minus Mr. Bourgon, for justified reason communicated to Chambers. Prosecution, Mr. Vanderpuye and Mr. McCloskey. So I think we can safely start. First thing before I ask if there are any preliminaries or whatever, yesterday in order to make it possible for all the staff for the sitting to finish more or less in time, and not disrupt the next sitting, we had not admitted, gone through the document admission. So we need to do that first and foremost. Mr. Vanderpuye, we start with you. We want to make sure of what you are tendering because some documents obviously formed part of the previous testimony of your witness, and I think we need to identify those this time. That's number 1. Second, then you made use of some documents in the course of his testimony and again those need to be admitted provided there are no valid objections. So let's start, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel, gentlemen. The exhibits that had been admitted pursuant to the prior testimony of the witness on 23rd May 2000 are as follows: First there is the transcript which is designated P02272 which I had asked to be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's admitted already.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Then there is a photograph -- I mean rather a map depicting the area of between Zvornik and Nova Kasaba with a yellow dot that was referred to in the testimony. That is designated P01470. There is also a photograph of a small brick shed with a red fence around it. That is designated P01921. Then there is another photograph of a road and a hill in the background. And that's referred to in the testimony as well and that's P01922. There is a photograph of the edge of the Jadar River, it's a bank, that is P01923. And then there is a Polaroid photograph of an entrance and exit wound, bullet wound, and that's designated P01924. I'm informed by our case manager that she was able to find a colour copy of that that I understand is appended to that exhibit as a second page. Those are the exhibits relevant to the prior testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And just for clarity's sake, when you say P01470, that's P01470 in this case and not in the previous case, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. I knew it was but I just want to avoid the possibility of a confusion later on. Yes. Then there is P02273 which is a pseudonym sheet under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct. And with respect to his testimony, in this proceeding, P01618 is a photograph of the area of Konjevic Polje that is unmarked. Then there was P02274 which was a marked version of the same photograph that the witness testified to and then PIC00031 was the same photograph with the markings that the witness then again marked in court. P01935 is a photo of a house in front of a -- in a small field that the witness referred to as well. P02275 is a photo with a couple of houses on a small field as well. And PIC00032 is the Polaroid photograph of the entrance and exit wound that the witness testified to prior but had been marked in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any objection from any of the Defence teams to the admission of any of these documents? Have you been given a copy of the coloured photo of the entry and exit wound?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That hasn't been provided to Defence counsel, but my understanding it's been uploaded to e-court so it's available to them for inspection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I take it there are no objections from anyone, so all these documents tendered are being admitted. Now, Defence documents. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. We would like to tender into evidence the document 5D89. It is handwritten declaration of the last witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Is it 5D89 or is it -- because what I have on my sheet of paper, I have 1D5D. It is 5D -- all right. So any objection from any of the Defence, other Defence teams or from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I think there was Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We would like to tender for admission two documents with numbers 5D85. Those are the discharge letters. We would like to tender pages 3 and 4 of that document. The first one is a discharge letter from the hospital, relative to the witness, dated 16 July 1995, and the second document is a letter to whom it may concern, from the medical centre, with the same date. Your Honour, there is a mistake in the translation but we will officially ask for a correction of that mistake from the translation service and then we will subsequently submit that correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Any objections from any of the other Defence teams or Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So these two pages will also be admitted. Madam Registrar, please put on record that both documents or Exhibit 1D5D89 and the newly admitted Exhibit 6D5D85 consisting of two pages will be kept under seal. Mr. Haynes or Mr. Sarapa, I don't know who is dealing with this, you also made use of some documents during your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. We would wish to tender into evidence two exhibits, please. The first, which -- and I understand the written notice is on its way to the Court manager, will be 7D55, which is a section of video, the ERN number of which is V0001357-1-A, from 27 minutes to 28 minutes. That's the video of the Orthodox Church and cemetery. And the second exhibit is 7D56, which is the order for mobilisation of able-bodied men between the ages of 16 and 60 which you will mark for identification purposes only because it is not yet translated into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could I ask you to repeat again, please, the video reference number? It's V.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it 1357 or 1375?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you check that because then it has been given wrongly to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, I'll certainly check that. I'm sure it is 1357.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's 3757, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Dash 1-A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that will be become 7D55?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections from any of the other Defence teams or Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So these two documents are also so admitted. That's it. To my knowledge, Mr. Meek or Mr. Stojanovic, I don't think you wish to tender any documents, do you? Or Madam Fauveau? All right. I think we can chose that chapter here. And before we bring in the next witness, are there any preliminary matters you wish to raise? Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. The outstanding question of protective measures and safe conduct for Witness 115. I can say having consulted all of my colleagues that there will be no objection to those applications. If you don't mind a little preamble, because I'm asked to say this, we collectively take the view that orders of this sort are generically intended to bring the best evidence out of witnesses and those that make these applications are in the best position to say whether they are required. And in such applications made by the Prosecution of this sort, we defer to their better judgement and respect the applications knowing that in due course, that respect and deference will be repaid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. McCloskey, are you in the mood of committing yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that was an offer and anything I say is going to be an acceptance, but I generally feel the same, so I don't think it should be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. From our position we only grant protective measures when we really are satisfied that the requirements of the law are met, and when in borderline cases, we usually take the step of interviewing the witness before he or she begins the testimony to make sure that it's a genuine case of -- and not something which is made up. So I think we can bring in the witness. You need to bring down the curtains. Now, for those of you who have not had courtroom practice before, this witness will be testifying with voice distortion. Now, it is important that throughout the entire testimony, when she is testifying, no one leaves his or her microphone on. All right? I will be keeping a lookout and I invite my colleagues to do the same, because it does happen many a time that someone does forget the microphone on, including ourselves sometimes, but please try to adhere strictly to this rule. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Madam. I wish to welcome you to this Tribunal and to this case on behalf of the Trial Chamber. This is the case against seven accused allegedly involved in the Srebrenica case. And you are about to start giving evidence very shortly, but before you do so, our rules require that you enter a solemn declaration to the effect that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Madam Usher, who is standing next to you will be handing to you the text of the solemn declaration. As soon as I finish talking, please read that declaration aloud, with the understanding that that will be your undertaking with us that you will be testifying the truth. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. Please take a seat. Make yourself comfortable. I'll explain to you a few other matters. Now, as I speak in English, whatever I am saying and for that matter whatever anyone else will be saying in the course of these proceedings, will be translated to you in your own language. If at any time you are not receiving interpretation or the interpretation you are receiving is not clear or not loud enough or too loud, please draw our attention straight away and we will see what we can do. Next thing I wanted to tell you is that the Prosecution has asked on your behalf for some protective measures to be put in place. We have carefully examined the case and we have agreed with the Prosecution to grant you protective measures. However, you may wish also to note that all the Defence teams agreed with the Prosecution that it is indeed the case of having these protective measures in place. These protective measures are the following: We have ordered that no one will be able to see your face while following these proceedings, of course, outside these four walls of this courtroom. If you look at your monitor, cameras are going to point on you and you will see how others will be seeing you from outside this courtroom. If the cameras could please focus on the witness. All right. This is how others will be seeing you. In addition, we have also decided to put in place voice distortion. While you testify, no one will be able to hear your true voice. Your voice will be distorted. And so no one would be able to recognise you from your voice. The third and also perhaps very important, if not the most important, precaution, protective measure we have put in place is to hide your name and surname, you're identity, and therefore no one will be referring to you by your name here and instead we will be using a number. And for all intents and purposes, in the records of this case, you will be known and referred to as Witness PW-125, 125. Of course, there will be moments when questions will be put to you that necessarily, by answering them, one would be able to identify you. In those cases, we will go into private session and that basically means that only the persons inside this courtroom will be able to follow the proceedings and nobody else outside this courtroom. I hope this puts your mind at rest and enables you to testify with relative ease and tranquillity and that these protective measures are to your satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So you are first going to be asked a series of questions by Mr. McCloskey who is lead counsel for the Office of the Prosecutor in this case. He will then be followed by each of the Defence teams, also, I assume. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you ready to give this a try?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. You've been able to take a deep breath and answer my questions and everyone's today. Okay. We'll start off by showing you a piece of paper with a name on it and if you could take a look at it and tell us if that's you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, if it is because you're rather tall, if it's more convenient for you to conduct your examination-in-chief sitting down so that you can switch on and off the microphone, we certainly have no objection or no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It's been many years since I've done that but I'll give it a try.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps you can show it to one of the Defence teams. I suppose you can assure the others that it is the correct name and let us have a look at it. Thank you. So that will be given a number later on, and it will be kept under seal, Madam Registrar. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go into private session for just the first few questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, your family is living in Srebrenica. Can you tell us what the conditions of living in Srebrenica were like in the weeks leading up before the attack on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: I don't understand. Are you talking about 1993 or 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good question. I'm talking about the -- what living was like before July 1995, say in May and June and July.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: The conditions were not good. There was no food. We did not have much to eat. There was no clothes or footwear. We suffered. Every day I went with my father from one house to another begging for a kilo of flour or beans. We were selling needles. We would make umbrellas using all the wire. We did not have footwear. I wore the same pair of slippers to go to school from Zelani Jadar to Srebrenica. It took me two hours in every direction. I walked over the stones. Sometimes I could not feel my feet. My feet were cut. There was no footwear. When it was raining, we would get to school in Srebrenica wet through. In a nutshell, the conditions were rather terrible, they were not good at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so you were 13 at about -- at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: I was 13 at the time when Srebrenica fell. At the age of 10, as a young girl, I left my home forever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what settlement were you living in in June, before Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: In Zelani Jadar a place called Slapovici. This was a camp, a settlement that was constructed by the Swedes. This is where we lived. And before that, we lived in Srebrenica, from 1993 to 1994, maybe, and we resided in the culture hall. This is the facility where we lived. This is where we had one room that 15 of us shared. We were thankful even for that room because there were people living on the roads. They did not have a roof over their heads. They had to sleep outside and cook outside. At least we had one room, although we used it to cook, sleep, wash there. This was all we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I want to take you now to July 1995 when the attack began on Srebrenica. What did you and your family do from Slapovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: We lived there up to 1995, up to the month of July, when the attack started. We lived there and we started fleeing towards Srebrenica. All the villages around us, Suceska and others, were moving towards Srebrenica. There was no where else to go. Srebrenica was the only place where we could go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why did you flee to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: Well, because there was shooting from all sides. We had to flee. We had to go somewhere, together with the rest of the people. We did not know what else to do. We were like in a hole, like in a pit. There was nowhere to go. We didn't know what to do, where to go. We just set off and hoped for the best.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: We were fleeing together with the rest of the people; we were not alone. There were other people fleeing towards Srebrenica. We arrived in Srebrenica in my aunt's house. There were shots from all over the place. This is where we found shelter. We spent a night there at my mother's aunt's place. On the following day, there was shelling and the window panes were broken on the house. We threw ourselves on the floor. My father covered my body so as to save me from the debris. At one point, people started running and shouting, "We have to flee. The Chetniks are coming to Srebrenica." And then all of a sudden, we started fleeing. Again we didn't know where to go. We went to the UNPROFOR to ask for help, for assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. When your father protected you from the glass, was that in an apartment in Srebrenica town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: Yes. Close to the town. Not in the very centre but the house is close to the town itself. Not in the very centre but very close to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say you went to UNPROFOR, was -- where was the location of the UNPROFOR that you went to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: They were in Srebrenica, in front of the post office building. We were moving towards them. There were a lot of people. The road was full of people. My brother and I got separated in that commotion, each of us went our separate ways. My mother and my father and my grandmother went yet another direction. As I was running, I saw a dead man on the street. I don't know whether he had been killed or what. We had to step over his body. Then we arrived in front of the post office building, in front of the UNPROFOR. People asked them to help them, and the UNPROFOR troops said that we should go back to our homes and they said that nothing would happen to us. As we started returning, below the hospital, we found our mother who had fainted because she didn't know where I and my brother were. This was a stream there. We did not have anything to put water into to help my mother. My brother took some water in his mouth and spit on her to help her, and then my father came. I don't know how the two of them had gotten separated in the first place, and where my grandmother was. Then we returned to the apartment where my maternal grandparents lived together with my mother's two brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you decide -- what did the family decide to do after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: We spent a night there. Again there were shots. We didn't know what to do. And in the morning, around 11.00, men, elderly and young and a few younger girls, decided to go through the woods. My brother and my father said that they would join them because everybody decided to go there. My mother gave them a loaf of bread each and we also had a kilo of salt and a kilo of sugar. That's what she put in their backpacks. We said goodbye to each other. Actually I said goodbye to my brother and my father. My mother didn't want to look at them because everybody knew that that goodbye would be a most difficult thing and they left. And a couple of hours later, we joined the rest of the people and went to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how did you get to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: There were a lot of people. We went along the road. We went down there. We were accommodated in the factories there. There were a lot of people. On the first day, there was shooting. As we were walking, we were not shelled directly but shells were falling around us. And when we arrived in Potocari, the first day was peaceful and calm. Nobody touched us. They did not enter the crowd of people. My uncle was with us. We found him in Potocari. And we also found my and my brother's friend. We entered the factory. We spent the night there although we didn't sleep. We were afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. That first day that you got to Potocari, did you see any Serb soldiers in Potocari around your factory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: No. Not on the first day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we go into private session just briefly again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, do you remember the -- that date, that first day that you actually -- that you walked with this group to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: It was the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I think you said you spent the night in that factory -- that night. Can you tell us what happened on the 12th of July briefly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: Well, on the 12th of July, I saw Serb soldiers. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: I don't know when this was. It was around noon, I would say. I don't know exactly how late it was. I was too afraid to look at the watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How many men took them away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: Two men came to take them away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how were those men dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: I don't know. I did not look at their clothes. I really can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: Well, the second night fell. My uncle returned. And that night, there was a lot of screaming around 2 or 3.00. After midnight, I could hear a lot of people screaming. And it's beyond words. I can't even begin to describe how terrible this was. That night was really, really terrible. When you hear maybe 30.000 people all screaming at the same time, there is just no way to describe that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were there Serb soldiers in the area on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: I saw them during the day, walking through the groups of people. They mingled with the people. During the night, I did not leave our factory. I did not see them inside the factory. And I don't know what the situation was outside. I don't know whether any of them were outside the factory where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened on the next day, the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: On the 13th of July, we decided to go because people started leaving towards Tuzla. My uncle was afraid because we had heard that men were being separated from the rest of the people. We at first wanted to linger on a little but then I said to my mother, "Mom, we have to go." Then we set off. We arrived there at the place we were supposed to be. There was a taped-off area and they were letting us go. There were buses there. They let me and my mother and my uncle go. My mother's parents and brother were not allowed to go with us in that -- and that group. And then when they let us go, they said to my uncle, "You have to step aside." He left and they told me, "You can't go either." And they allowed my mother to go to the lorries that were there. As for my uncle, we never saw him again. We just saw him being taken to the side, as had been ordered. My mother and I started crying. We asked -- we started pleading with them to let me go together with my mother. There was a group of those Chetniks, I don't know what to call them. That's the name I heard. We were both crying and they repeated that I couldn't go, that my mother should go, and my mother said, "I have only her. Please let her go. I don't have anybody else." And then an UNPROFOR soldier came. My mother pleaded with him. And she was telling him, "Please let her go. I don't have anybody but her." She was crying all the while. Then he went up there to them to ask them again, this was not approved, and then one person from that group said, "Okay. Let's let her go. She is a child." And the other cursed him and said, "Look at the little girl. She is so beautiful." Then my mother and I started walking towards the lorries. And I was saying to my mother, "Please, hurry up, mom. The lorries are leaving." And she said to me, "I can't let them kill us both." And as we got on the lorry, my mother fainted and never came to until the moment we arrived at the place where we were being taken to. There was an old lady who had some water and used that water to help my mother, to cool her off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you said there was a Dutch soldier, I think, that your mother pleaded with. And did you say that Dutch soldier went over and talked to the Chetniks or the Serbs? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam, if at any time it becomes difficult for you to continue testifying and you need a little bit of a break, please tell us straight away and we will have a short break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Another deep breath. And were you and your mother able to take the bus and eventually walk to Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: Yes. We got on to the truck and then we reached Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And since those days, have you ever seen your father or your uncle or your brother alive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: No. Never again. We hoped every day, waited for them to come. When we just arrived, I went from Tuzla to Dubrava where people were crossing over, and I waited, but we never found out anything about them until they were identified, and that's when all hope died for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've told me that they were able to find your uncle's remains in Pilica and your father's in Cerska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you see a -- if we could go into private session just briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. And if I could just reiterate my recommendation that as soon as you finish your question, you switch off the microphone, please. Thank you. One moment. Madam, Mr. Zivanovic is appearing for Colonel Popovic in this case and he will be cross-examining you first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let's go into private session for a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, since we were in private session, the totality of Mr. Zivanovic's cross-examination of the witness was conducted in private session. Who is going next? Mr. Meek is representing Colonel Beara and he will be -- or I don't know if he will be cross-examining you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. We have no questions for this witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Meek. Madam Nikolic is representing Lieutenant Nikolic in this case and let's see if she is cross-examining you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. We have no questions for this witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Nikolic. Mr. Lazarevic is appearing for General Borovcanin in this case. And he will be cross-examining or --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No. This witness does not call for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Madam Fauveau is representing General Miletic in this case. Go ahead and please, your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, you mentioned the conditions prevailing in Srebrenica in 1995. You said that they were very bad. Can we say that in 1993, when you arrived in Srebrenica, the conditions were just as bad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: Yes. In 1993 -- from 1993 to 1995 the conditions were difficult for food, clothing, footwear. If any convoy did happen to arrive in Srebrenica, it would be coincidental. They were stopping and preventing convoys from reaching Srebrenica and perhaps all we would receive would be two kilograms of flour, to cover five members of our family. That would be all.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When in Potocari you were able to get on a bus with your mother, you were relieved, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: The fear and everything that my mother and I experienced cannot be described. But when I got into the truck, I in a way escaped from what possibly could have happened to me, but my mother couldn't come to until we reached our territory, but still during the trip itself, a person didn't know what could happen. Something could have happened on the trip also.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that when you got to Kladanj, you were relieved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-125
utterances.text: Yes. When I crossed into our territory, when we arrived, we were not completely on our territory. We also had to go through Serb territory and then when we did cross into our territory, we did feel relief, but then there was pain too because we thought that our dear ones had come too but then when we saw that they were not there, then there was terrible pain, suffering, crying.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau. Mr. Josse or Mr. Krgovic, are you cross-examining the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We have no questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And Mr. Krgovic represents General Gvero here. And Mr. Haynes or Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your Honour, nor I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And Mr. Haynes represents General Pandurevic. Is there re-examination by any chance?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam, that fortunately brings your testimony to an end here, which means that you are free to go back to your residence. Our staff will be assisting you to facilitate your return back home at the earliest. On behalf of my colleagues, Judge Kwon, Judge Prost and Judge Stole, I wish to thank you for having come over to give testimony. And on behalf of everyone here, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Make sure there is no broadcasting of her going out. So, documents or exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The pseudonym sheet, P02276 and the one still, P02277.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. He only made use of one, I think. He made -- 78, 02278. But you're tendering also --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, I think one is enough. I didn't want to do the second one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The one you used is 02278.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So any objection? None? So the -- both the pseudonym sheet and P2278 are being admitted and both will be kept under seal. Yes. I think it's the case of taking a break now. One thing for the record, because it occurred to me sometime during the night. Yesterday, when Mr. Vanderpuye sought to introduce the transcripts of that witness's previous testimony, inadvertently I may have mentioned that it was being admitted under Rule 92 ter instead of Rule 89(F). I may have made that mistake. I know that it was tendered under 89(F). So for the record, I am correcting myself and the record. Thank you. The break needs to be of 30 minutes because of the redactions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we start with the next witness, it has been brought to our attention, and Mr. McCloskey, correct me if I'm wrong, that in our decision of the 23rd of August, we went beyond what you requested by way of protective measures for this new witness; namely, you had requested pseudonym and facial distortion, which we granted, but we also granted, for reasons that here and now I cannot explain, it probably was an oversight, voice distortion. That's our decision which we would very quickly be prepared to vary if you stick or you declare that you stick to your original request.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. He think we can stick to the original request. I have discussed that with the witness and I think he's okay with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So having heard Mr. McCloskey, we vary our decision of the 23rd of August 2006, in which we had granted the following protective measures to Witness PW-113; namely, the use of a pseudonym and facial and voice distortion, by retaining only the use of pseudonym and facial distortion. There will no longer be voice distortion. So thank you. You can admit the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir, and welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have testified already before this Tribunal in another case, so more or less you should be familiar with the procedure, even though a few years have passed since your last testimony here. Madam Usher, who is standing right next to you, will be handing you the text of the solemn declaration. Once you have read it out aloud, that would become your solemn undertaking with this Tribunal, that in the course of your testimony, you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. So please proceed with the reading of that solemn declaration and we can start with your testimony soon after.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take a seat. Make yourself comfortable. There are a couple of things that I need to explain to you before you start giving evidence, and first is the following: Sometime back, Mr. McCloskey, who is lead counsel for the Prosecution in this case, asked us to issue, to grant, some protective measures. The idea being to hide, to protect your identity, to hide your identity from the world outside this courtroom, which would enable you to testify with greater ease. The protective measures that were asked from us were the following: First, that we would never use your name here and that you will be referred to and identified as with a pseudonym and we have granted that. No one will refer to you by your name. You will be referred to by a pseudonym, and you, for the records, you will be known as Witness PW-113. The Prosecution also asked that to further protect your identity, we should put in place a system whereby no one could see your face while you testify here, and we have granted that. So you will be testifying with facial distortion. If the technicians kindly focus the camera on you, and if you look at your monitor, this is how you will appear to the outside world. No one will be able to see your face, but only a set of coloured squares. Of course, in the course of the testimony, there will be questions which you will be required to answer, and by answering those questions, your identity could be revealed. In those instances, we will go into so-called private session. I suppose you are used to this as well. Basically this means that what is being said while the private session is on will only and can only be heard by the persons inside this courtroom and, of course, the technicians who are -- and interpreters who are working behind the glass panels that you see on either side of the courtroom. No one else will be able to hear what is being said while we are in private session. Again, that is another mode which we will be putting in place to protect your identity. First of all, is that to your satisfaction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. McCloskey will go first. He will be examining you. However, since -- any way, I'll leave you in the hands of Mr. McCloskey. He will be followed subsequently by the various Defence teams on cross-examination, something which each accused is entitled to do. So if at any moment you require a break, please do tell us, don't hesitate, and we will grant you a break. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. First let's start out. I've got a piece of paper that I want you to look at and tell us if this person on the paper is you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes, this is me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's 65 ter P02279. Now, in the last couple of days, did you have a chance to have testimony from a Blagojevic trial read back to you in your own language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as far as you know, was that the entire -- your entire testimony from that trial?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes. That was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you point out two mistakes in that testimony to me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And aside from that, can you declare that the information in that transcript accurately reflects your declaration on the subjects?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes. It is accurate save for those two mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And if you were asked the same questions today, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: They would be, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just go to the mistakes briefly and deal with them. If we could go to -- I'll just go to page 1418, lines 2 and 3, and I'll just say this for the record. It says, in English, "that I looked after the flat of you and your mothers and I protected it and you're killing innocent people." The mistake that was pointed out by the witness is that what he really said was, "I looked after your mother, Stana, and you, and protected her." The word for "flat" in Bosnian is similar to Stan or Stana and that's just the mistake as he explained it with the interpreter. And the second mistake is on page 1423, and that is when he was telling about where he was going after the executions, and I think I'll have him clear up that mistake after I read the summary of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Which means you can proceed with the reading of the summary straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could go into private session just for the first couple of lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "This witness is a Bosnian Muslim. He was 17 years old in July 1995. Prior to the war, he lived with his family in the village of Nova Kasaba." Now, I think we can go into open after now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's revert to open session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "After the occupation of Cerska and Konjevic Polje, his family moved to the area around Srebrenica. "From about the beginning of July, there was shelling every day, and on about 11 July, the witness, his father, his mother and three sisters decided they had to leave their home. They set off together to the village of Suceska where they split up. The witness and his father went through the woods to the village of Jaglici and his mother and sisters went towards the UN base in Potocari. "The witness decided to go with his father because, and I quote, 'I wasn't sure that UNPROFOR would protect us, certainly not the men, considering all the experience in the war and knowing what the Serb army had doing -- had been doing.'" That's page 1381, line 20 to 22. "On the 11th of July, in the afternoon, there were about 10 to 15.000 people, predominantly men, including young men, and some women and children, in the area. The column of people organised before dark but he became separated from his father in the large crowd. The witness has not seen his father since that time. Soldiers went ahead in the column while most of the civilians stayed behind with a group of armed soldiers remaining behind. He set off in the morning with the column. "As the column moved forward on the 12th, it was shelled throughout the day and there were increasingly more injured people who were crying for help but were left in the woods. During the night of the 12th, the people were also fired upon. On the morning of the 13th, the witness noticed five or six people around him that had been killed, and many people in the group were confused and scared. The witness estimated he saw about 300 to 500 dead people in the woods that day. "At about 10 a.m. Serb soldiers were speaking over loudspeakers saying the Muslims should surrender and threatening to shell them if they did not surrender. The Serb soldiers stated they would be treated according to the Geneva Conventions. The witness followed the people through the woods and the people started surrendering. The witness came out by the asphalt road and saw five or six soldiers telling people to surrender and give up their bags, gold, deutschmarks. They insisted on the money more than anything else. He was told to put his bag of belongings near a tank by the asphalt road. "Prior to the time everyone came from the woods, the Serb soldiers behaved very properly. But when everybody had surrendered, the Serb soldiers started to mistreat people. They started cursing and saying, 'Fuck your balija mother' and asking for money again. The witness saw another armoured weapon with a machine-gun mounted on it with the words, 'Queen of death' written in the Cyrillic alphabet. The group of Muslims he was with was forced to move along the road to a meadow near the village of Sandici where there was a tank. On the way to the meadow the witness saw a dead body in civilian clothes and he saw buses with Muslim women and children in them driving in the direction of Konjevic Polje. "The witness estimated about 2.000 Muslims were present at that meadow. At about 5 p.m., a soldier at the meadow told everyone they would be taken to hangars in Bratunac and exchanged. The Serbs also said that anyone born in 1980 or after was allowed to leave. Three boys stood up and were allowed to leave. Others who stood up or raised their hands were not allowed to leave. The witness was with his uncle who told him to raise his hand but the witness did not dare because the soldier had told the previous child that he could not go. The witness's uncle did not survive. "The witness and others were then required to lay on their stomachs and with their hands behind their necks. After about three hours, several large trucks arrived and the people were loaded on to them. The witness was ordered on to the last truck. The truck was covered with a tarpaulin and it was extremely crowded and hot inside. People were jammed together so nobody could sit down. The truck drove to Bratunac and parked there overnight. The witness and others were held on the truck. It was unbearable. The witness couldn't feel anything, his whole body became numb. They asked for water but were told to be quiet and cursed at. "The next morning the truck set off with other trucks. People on his truck said they saw an UNPROFOR APC but he did not see it. Just outside Bratunac, the trucks stopped and people in his truck were given a small amount of water. They waited there for about two hours until about 10.00 a.m. or later, but still in the morning. And then the trucks set off again in the direction of Konjevic Polje and then in the direction of Zvornik. The trucks drove through Zvornik and Karakaj and turned left and on to a school building with a concrete playing field. He and others in the truck had to stay in the truck for about an hour. The conditions in the truck were unbearable. People were screaming for water and one man drank his own urine. "When the witness was allowed off the truck, he and others were directed to walk down the steps into the building and soldiers were standing on both sides of the steps hitting the people as they went by and cursing them. Once inside the building, the group went up some stairs. As they were going up the stairs, a Serbian soldier said, 'Whose land is this, this is Serbian land and will always remain so.' And the group had to repeat this after him. At the top of the stairs, they turned left to a hall way and walked down the hallway to one of the classrooms. There were about four or five classrooms along the hallway and there was noise from people inside those other classrooms. "The conditions in the classrooms was very bad. They were not allowed to go to the toilet and most everyone was soaked with urine. They were given a small amount of water but everyone remained very thirsty. The air in the classroom was hot and hard to breathe and when someone tried to open a window, shots rang out breaking windows and wounding five or six men. His group was making a lot of noise and the soldiers guarding them pointed out two young men and said they would be killed unless the group was quiet. A soldier came in the classroom and asked the group if there was anyone from Cerska, Konjevic Polje, Glogova or Osmace and other villages. Some men raised their hands and were taken outside the classrooms and beating could be heard. Those men never returned. "When darkness fell, the witness could hear soldiers telling people in other classrooms to come out, two or three at a time. Gun fire was then heard reverberating in the hallway. At about midnight, someone said the people in the classroom would be going out for an examination of some kind and he also mentioned being exchanged. "The witness said, before -- before that, and I quote, 'Before that people were talking amongst themselves and it was clear to us that they were killing people from the other classrooms. That it would be better for us if we all ran out at the same time. They couldn't kill everyone. Because they were so -- because there were many more of us in comparison with the soldiers, although they had weapons. Many people didn't want to do that. They said maybe we'll survive. We shouldn't run out. Nobody wanted to die.'" That's at page 1408, line 21 through 25 and 1409, lines 1 to 2. "The witness and the others were led from the classroom and ordered to remove their shoes and shirts. Their hands were tied behind their backs and they were pushed into a dark classroom until everyone in his group had their hands tied. Then they went down the stairs and outside. The witness could feel stuff sticking to his feet as he walked by dead people in front of the school. He and others were placed in the back of the truck and people started screaming and shots were fired and people were falling over each other. The truck drove to a location about ten minutes away. First along an asphalt road, then along a macadam road that caused the truck to shake. The truck stopped and he could hear bursts of fire next to the truck. People were taken off his truck, five at a time. One man tried to run away and shots were fired as he ran. After that, a Muslim started to shout and scream and said, 'I looked after your mother, Stana, and protected her and now you're killing innocent people.' "When the witness's turn came, he jumped off the truck and was told to find a spot among the rows of dead people. He found a place to stand and was told to lie down. As the witness fell forward, shots rang out and he felt pain to his elbow and to his right side of his chest. The witness stayed still on the ground and the firing continued around him and he was hit with something in the foot. The soldier called out that anyone who was still warm needs a bullet in his head. The man lying next to the witness was shot in the head at close range by a soldier. As people were being killed around him, the witness's biggest worry was that his mother would never know where he was. "Eventually the soldiers left and he and another survivor were able to partially untie each other and escape the area, just as another truck was arriving. The witness and his companion spent the night in a concrete canal or ditch nearby while the killing continued. At daybreak, they started to walk away and discovered that there was a dam above the plateau where the killing had occurred. They were also able to see a loader loading the bodies in the morning. "The witness and his companion wandered for several days and were eventually able to make it back to Muslim territory." I'll go to the mistake that I said I would. That's the end of the summary. To clear it up. It's at page 1423, line 10. Well I'll start a little earlier to put it in context. This is the next day. The witness says, "And when we climbed to the top of the hill, we saw that above the plateau where all the killing went on. Above the plateau down the dam, later on I saw it was a dam, on the other side of that dam, there was a guard with a rifle and we couldn't go anywhere. We had to go down back to the canal and across those dead."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, did I just read the mistake that you pointed out to us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Could you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah. "And we couldn't go anywhere and we had to go down back to the canal and across those dead. We had to go to another hill."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: When we went to this ditch, we had to actually get to a hill to see where we were. And then when we came back, we didn't step over the dead because there were several levels on the dam so that we passed but we didn't see the dead. There were dead bodies but we knew where they were so we kind of passed around them and took the field, the meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And in your testimony, as I quoted, you said, "I wasn't sure that UNPROFOR would protect us, certainly not the men, considering all the experience in the war and knowing what the Serb army had been doing." Can you briefly tell us of any experiences or incidents that occurred during the war that you were referring to with this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: At the very beginning of the war, before we left our homes, we heard that the serious -- the Serb army had committed serious crimes in the villages of Bratunac, in Glogova, in the school that people were being detained at the stadium in Bratunac. My uncle also lived in Bratunac so we were worried about him. That they had started to expel and detain people in Vlasenica and also another village Zagore near Vlasenica; it's about 15 kilometres approximately away. The Serbs had killed 100 people. They simply summoned them. I heard that from people who came later, people who survived. They simply summoned them as if they had something to tell them and then they killed them there. So this changed our view. We really couldn't trust the Serbian army any more. Secondly, when I was still in school in Kasaba, the Serb soldiers, or the reservists who were on their way to Croatia, would pass through and fire at Muslim houses, Muslim houses. They killed about 100 people in Glogova and that actually changed our opinion, and people started to flee to the woods. They didn't trust the Serbs any more. And then later, this had an influence on our escape from Cerska and later when we were going to Srebrenica, and also when I was making my decision whether to go to Potocari or to go through the woods. I couldn't, in view of all of these experiences and those of my neighbours who had stayed in these villages and they are no longer here today, in 1992, 1993, I couldn't trust them. So I decided to go through the woods because of these experiences and the experiences with UNPROFOR, because the UNPROFOR actually danced to the Serbs' tune, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And can you, and very briefly, explain how you were assisted from the killing fields by a companion? Of course, don't name that person, but could you just very briefly tell us how you were helped by this man and how you made it. But briefly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I never believed I would survive. I was wounded, and I was in pain, in a lot of pain. Just one moment, please. I was seriously wounded and I was just waiting to die. I didn't even think that I could escape or that I would go anywhere. While I was suffering and lying like that, I could see a man moving around amongst the dead and I asked him if he was alive and he said yes, and he called to me to come to untie him and I just simply couldn't. This lasted for hours. And he couldn't move until I came. I kind of rolled to reach him. I would roll once and then wait for half an hour. And he didn't need to pull my ropes off with his teeth. It was already loose. The soldier who tied my hands didn't tie them tightly. And then we could see some vehicle approaching, a truck or something, or a tractor. We could tell by the sound that something like that was approaching. And it was dark. And he managed to stand up and to go off while he was still tied and I also thought that I would go but I was actually just crawling over the dead and then I lowered myself into the ditch. In the meantime a truck had arrived. The person had a T-shirt so he dressed my wounds. We didn't even know each other. He dressed my wounds. And then all I recall is that he called to me, "It's daylight. We have to go." And then we wandered around for days, for days. We didn't even think we could cross over. He was able to walk. We simply went from one day to the next until we met a mine or a soldier or something. He would go about ten metres in front of me and he was removing the grass. I would be crawling, then I would want to give up, then he would come to me and beg me and I said, "I can't go on. If you want, you can leave me."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, please could you ask him whether he needs a short break? Do you want to stop for a while?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no need. I just need a moment. I don't need to go out. If I can just have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was so persistent, he would come to me, he would beg me, "You have to go, you have to go" even though we didn't know where we were going. We were just wandering around, wandering through villages, Serb villages, sleeping. I was cold. I was half dressed in bare feet. If we passed through a graveyard or something, he would take the shirt off from the cross and give it to me to wear. I was hungry, exhausted. He would carry me for a while. Then after four days of wandering, we just incidentally crossed into a Muslim village. Only he knows how much I suffered. I wouldn't wish that upon anyone. I wished to die a thousand times. I wished that. I would have preferred for the soldiers to have killed me but I just couldn't summon them -- I just kept telling him, you go on, leave me. But he was so persistent and we did manage to finally cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for one second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I want to go over some pictures, if we could just ask to you identify these pictures. I know you've been shown them many times over the years, but if we could start with 65 ter 1729. And do you recognise this photo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: This is the entrance in front of the school where we were brought to in the truck from the direction of Bratunac. This school is close to Zvornik. This is where we got off the trucks, and this is the school where we were before they took us to the execution. This is the entrance where the beatings took place, and where probably the killings took place when we were in the classrooms. Later I saw piles of people, but I was just walking, keeping my head down. I wasn't really thinking about anything. They were my last moments. But this is the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next shot, which is 65 ter 1730. What is this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: This is the inside of the school and these are the steps that we took. This is where we were detained. We were on the first floor, and you can see a part of the floor where we were. You can see the door behind which we were being held.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next shot, 65 ter 1731. What's this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: This is the floor of the school where we were detained. These are the classrooms. I was in the last or the last but one. I'm not sure. I was in either one of those. This is the hall where we were taken out later when we were tied, where our clothes were removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say the last, are you talking about the farthest away in this picture as shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes. It's farther away. Perhaps you can't even see that door here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next picture, 65 ter 1737. What's this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: This is actually the place where we were brought to in the truck, and this is where the killings were done. This place where you can see some people standing, that's where the truck was and where the killings were committed. We fled below and into the woods that you can see right there, and then the next day, after the execution, we were there and we could see a guard walking up and down the dam with a rifle. We were trying to see where we could go. Actually, my friend was looking where we could go. I was just lying down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next shot, which is 65 ter 1739. What's this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: This is the concrete ditch into which I crawled after my friend stood up and left. This is where we hid. And we left this ditch later and from there we went into the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go now to 65 ter 1908. These will be some -- just a few photographs of some injuries. Is this an injury to your foot sustained during the executions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes. This is the wound on the sole of my foot when I was lying down, when they were firing at the lines behind me and this hit me in the foot when I was already lying down. This is probably fragmentation ammunition. I still have metal fragments in my -- in the sole of my foot. They still haven't been removed from that time. This photograph was taken two or three months or even later after I was actually wounded. I'm not sure when it was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 1910. What's this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: These are my wounds on my right side and also on my arm, on the elbow, from the bullets that I was hit with. Perhaps they are not visible but you can't really see them all that well, but this photograph was also taken a few months after I was wounded. These were also probably fragmentation bullets because I still have other places in my body where the bullets passed through. I have a lot of fragments still in my stomach and in my arm from those bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. These two photos, 1908 and 1909 which also have an ERN number, are they material of common domain? In other words, if someone wants to look up these two photos -- maybe they are accompanied by a description of who they refer to. If someone could help me on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: They are in the Srebrenica-specific area of the EDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But they wouldn't be accompanied by a description indicating --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't think so, no. Not in -- not where they are stored, but I think there is -- our counsel have that but no one else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I feel safe, if that's the position. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In any case, I'm told that they were not broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know if there is a mistake in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey referred to the last two photographs as 65 ter 1908 and 1910 and you referred to them as 1908 and 1909.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey is right. 1909 is also a photograph of the injuries on the shoulder and chest of the witness. While 19 it says "above but frontal view of injuries on chest." So I assume that it was 1910 which was used and not 1909. I didn't check but I take it that Mr. McCloskey knew what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is one of the times I did, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's why I didn't check on you because I felt it was like that. Now we are coming to the cross-examination. Who is going first? Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We shan't cross-examine this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Zivanovic is lead counsel defending accused Colonel Popovic in this case and he's chosen not to cross-examine you. Who is next? Mr. Meek is representing Colonel Beara in this case and he will be cross-examining you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I just have a few questions for you. You've testified before. We know that. And you've given quite a few statements; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In the statement that you gave, several statements, you talked about ambushes during the time that the column was moving from Susnjari to the free territory. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours. This cord is not very long for me, so I'm doing the best I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It's a fact, isn't it, Witness, that you described the column that was moving from Susnjari towards the free territory as at times members of that column were committing suicide and even arguing with each other and shooting and killing each other; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: No. It's not all correct. It's correct but I will explain to you what is correct. In the statement it's all correct, yes, they were arguing, killing each other, committing suicide, I don't know to what extent, but actually the situation was so difficult and unbearable, so the -- they couldn't stand it. That's the reason for the suicides. Many of them had lost their minds. Some of them did not want to give themselves up, and that was the reason for the suicides. The situation was so unbearable that this is understandable. What you're saying about them killing each other, there is a sentence there that says they started to argue and kill each other. You could understand that in different ways. Actually that they were killing themselves, not that they were killing each other. That's, I think, a sufficient explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I can appreciate that, Witness. My next question is: Can you give me an estimate as to the number of individuals in that column that either died by suicide or died by being shot by a fellow Muslim that was in that column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question, what you wanted to say. Could you please just explain it a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I will. You've just testified that during the column, the march towards the free territory, that you witnessed incidents of suicide by people in the column. You also testified that --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: -- you also witnessed incidents where individuals, because of the intolerable situation and some wanting to surrender, some not, that they shot each other, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Can you please read those sentences from my statement, as they are there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please do, if you are insisting pursuing this matter, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I can insist, Your Honour, but he's already indicated, and I can go back to his direct examination, his cross-examination, if you give me just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just -- I'm just appealing to you to make things easy, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: This would be a statement July 19th 1995. You state, "I stayed in the woods with the others for one day and one night. The Chetniks kept shelling the place with Pragas and other weapons." Then you say, "That day, people started arguing and killing each other. Some wanted to surrender and others did not." Do you remember that statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: It says they were killing each other. Is that exactly what it says, "killing each other"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That is verbatim from the English translation. I can have my colleague who is fluent in B/C/S look at the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes, you can. You mentioned Muslims killing each other, and I don't remember ever having mentioned the word "Muslim" in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You didn't, Witness. I'm just telling you, that in your statement of the 19th of July, you were speaking of what transpired and what occurred in the column that was moving from Susnjari to Tuzla. Okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying and where you're coming from but can you please read back to me the sentence as I said it, verbatim? You don't have to explain things to me. Just read it back to me. Maybe you can give it to me to read the sentence, just that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I apologise. And, Mr. President, Your Honours, I would ask permission of the Court to let my colleague, Mr. Mrkic read that sentence in B/C/S and have it translated or I can show it to him. It's outlined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's show it to the witness straight away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or maybe that passage, please, not just witness sentence, maybe two or three sentences preceding it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does the statement have that paper itself --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: This is highlighted, that's all, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's put it on the ELMO for everyone to be able to read, but if it has the witness's name on it, then we go in private session for one moment or make sure that it is not broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not very legible, but I'll do my best. Can I start reading?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "On that day, people started quarrelling amongst each other, and killing each other." I said that this may be ambiguous but I'm here to explain things. I didn't see anybody killing each other but some people committed suicide by hand grenades. Maybe there were people wounded. But I never -- didn't see anybody actually kill somebody else, and it doesn't say that people killed each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, could you go ahead and read the next sentence so that we can see if the translation is any different? Just read it out loud so the translators can also then translate it into English.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: "On that day, people started quarrelling amongst each other and killing each other. Some wanted to surrender, the others didn't. At one point, a column set off towards the village of Sandici and I joined the column together with my uncle."

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Shall I go on reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, you've read that out in your own language, B/C/S, your own statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And in English, it came through that "on that day, people started quarrelling amongst each other and killing each other."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But he's given an explanation. He's explained it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: How many people then -- you're saying they didn't kill each other, they just committed suicide, is that what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we should labour it and belabour it. He said that he saw several or some people committing suicide using hand grenades and, in the process, some others may have been injured or even killed, but he did not see anyone specifically killing someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Fair enough, Your Honour, fair enough. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, approximately how many people did you see die in that manner during those days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: In what manner? By people committing suicide or in the way that you want me to say that they were killing each other? What do you mean when you say "by that manner"? Are you referring to hand grenades? What?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, I suggest to you, unless you really want a head-on collision with some members of the Defence teams, that you try to cooperate with us. Mr. Meek here has got every right to ask questions, and you have a responsibility also pursuant to the solemn declaration that you made earlier on, you have a responsibility and an obligation, a legal obligation, as well as a moral one, to answer his questions. So please don't try to enter into an argumentation with Mr. Meek or, for that matter, anyone else that will be asking you questions. If you want to distinguish between those who according to you committed suicide and those who were injured by the grenades used by others in committing suicide, you are entitled to do so, but please don't argue with counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not arguing. He can ask me whatever he wants. I'm trying to answer his questions. And I have already answered his question, and I said that I had seen several people who committed suicide. And that is my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But do you have a number, an approximate number? This is what he's asking you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I wouldn't be able to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, Witness -- and, certainly, I'm not here to argue with you by any means. In your various statements, you testified that while the column was moving from Susnjari towards the free territory, that there were ambushes that had occurred; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And could you just tell me to the best of your ability how you would define an ambush?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I can't define an ambush, but I can tell you how it was so you can draw your own definition, if you will. There were a lot of people, and the column was long, and I was towards its end with the majority of civilians. On day 1, there was no shooting, no shelling and as we were walking through the forest, all of a sudden shelling started, and this was very hard to bear. There was shooting from different types of weaponry, a lot of people were wounded. Nobody helped each other because we just couldn't. And all of a sudden the column came to a halt. It could not go on moving because there was an ambush ahead of us and the Serb army had cut off the column and we could not go any further. And that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Witness, there has been testimony in this courtroom that there was -- there were men with weapons in that column, some testimony even indicating maybe a third of the men had weapons of some sort, hunting rifles, deer rifles, shot guns, hand guns and grenades. Further, there has been evidence in this courtroom, that some of the armed men were in the front of the column and some armed men were towards the rear of the column. Now, since you just testified that you were towards the rear of the column or the end of the column, were there men from the ABiH army, whether they were in civilian clothes or not, who had weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
