utterances.text: As we were entering the forest, in my group or in my part of the column, which was huge - I don't know how many kilometres long - most people with me were civilians because the army would not let us go in the front of the column. They wanted us to go in the rear of the column. And I only saw a few troops there. As we entered the forest, confusion started. There were a lot of dead and wounded and the whole thing broke apart and I did see a soldier here and there, but very few of them. Most of the soldiers went ahead of the column, so it may be the case that the Serbs did it on purpose to let the military through and then stop the civilians or as they called us, unarmed soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you just testified that as you entered the forest you saw a lot of dead and wounded. Can you give the Court an estimate of how many dead that you observed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: When the shelling started, when the general attack started, according to my estimate, the column was cut off and it's very difficult for me to estimate. I don't know who would be able to give you an estimate, but I believe that some 300 to 500 people, maybe less, maybe more, but approximately that many. As I was walking through the forest, as I was fleeing, jumping over dead bodies, I would say that that is as many as I saw but this is only my estimate. There was a lot of wounded and the number of wounded, maybe even surpassed the number of those who were not wounded and I'm talking only about my part of the column and to what I saw was happening around me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And as you went through the forest, some of the dead or wounded that you observed would have been dead or been wounded previous to that, by further up in the column and stayed where they were, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand your question fully. Are you asking me whether all the wounded remained there or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No. Let me rephrase the question. As far as some of the dead that you observed along the route that you took, you didn't observe all of them being killed while in your presence, but they were there when you went by them. Am I correct about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: As I was passing through, I could see shell shrapnel. On some bodies I couldn't even discern wounds but they were dead. Some people lost their legs or arms. There was such a state of confusion, and it happened so fast that nobody actually paid much attention to anybody else. Fathers would leave their wounded sons behind as a result of this unbearable state of confusion and panic. And the shelling was so intense that it could not be borne any more. The Serbs just wanted to kill us all and we had a choice either to surrender or they would have killed us all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And again, that choice to surrender or not caused some arguments and some people in that column died because of those arguments; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: People argued as to whether to surrender or not. Those who wanted could surrender. Those who didn't want could only flee somewhere or if they had a hand grenade or a piece of weaponry they could kill themselves, but those people were rare. Some of the soldiers who were left behind fled. I saw some people in the forest, even those who did not bear arms, who did not want to continue with the convoy, they just surrendered. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you, sir, about the school, and on the 31st day of July of 1995, you gave a statement in Tuzla, and on the statement, you state, that later on you were transported and then you say, "I saw under the canvass that they had brought us to a school in Petkovici." Do you remember making that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: It is true, but I think I can guess what you're trying to ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to ask you because on the 24th day of July 1995, a week earlier than that, you made a statement about the Petkovici school where you stated that you "later learned the school was in Petkovici." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: What was said in this other statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That you "later learned the school was in Petkovici."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes. Before that, I did not even know that that was a school. It was only when we entered that we saw school boards and similar things by which I could tell that this was a school. I didn't know what the name of the school was. Later on I heard from people either there or as we were walking through the village, that this was a school -- the school in Petkovci. That is why I provided that in my statement. I said that I was in the school in Petkovci. This is the only explanation I can give you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, Witness, you had a proofing session in 2003 prior to your testimony, before testimony in Blagojevic case. You recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: What proofing session are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you. Before your testimony today, did you meet with Mr. McCloskey and go over previous statements, previous testimony, and what your testimony would be today? That's what I mean by a proofing session.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And do you recall doing that on the 20th of July 2003, with an investigator from the ICTY, from the Office of the Prosecutor, before you testified in 2003?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I suppose I did but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, let me just try to refresh your recollection. You told that investigator that there was a mistake on the statement dated 19 July 1995, which you gave to the officer of the BiH army, the organ of military security service. You stated that in page 2 of that statement, it had been written, "A total of about 600 of us surrendered." I believe that you told that investigator on July 20, 2003, that you never said those words, that it was probably added by the officer who had interviewed you and since today you had never seen this statement and had had no possibility to correct it. Does that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I may have said it but I can't remember, so I can't answer your question, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you answer --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I can't answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's fair. Can you tell me approximately how many surrendered when you did, if not 600, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: It's very difficult to assess, given the length of the column, the large number of wounded, the forest. If you were to observe the situation from an aircraft or a helicopter, then you could tell. I can only tell you how many I saw in the meadow or on the asphalt road, and this is what I can base my estimates on. And it was a long time ago. I can tell you how many of us there were in total. There were some 1.000 to 2.000 on the asphalt and in the meadow, later on, when we were running but that doesn't have to mean that we all came at the same time. It does not have to mean that we all surrendered at the same time, that everybody surrendered together with us. Bear in mind that the column was really long. So there may have been people preceding us in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that, Witness. I just want to know if a total of 600 of us surrendered in your group or close to the time you did, is not a correct number, what is a correct number? If you can tell us today, that you saw and observed surrendering when you did.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I've just answered that question, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. I'll move on. I just want to know, didn't you have orders from the army command, and that's why you went with your father and other able-bodied men to Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I believe that I said enough at the beginning. I didn't opt for the UNPROFOR. I knew that we couldn't be safe there. My cousins, who were able-bodied and who were not able-bodied went to Potocari and are no longer with us. They were killed. In other words, they knew that they would be killed either if they went to Potocari or through the forest. I just made an attempt through the forest hoping that I would survive. I am amongst the living today but I suffered greatly, and please let me answer -- let me complete my answer. It if you don't allow me to complete my answer, I don't think I can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's not answering. He's being-- I asked him a specific question, whether or not, you know, there was a command from the army for able-bodied people to go to Susnjari and he's not answering that question. He's being unresponsive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It was a compound question which has got us into that trouble and I didn't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest that we have the break now, straight away. We'll give the witness a break. In the meantime think about what I'm going to suggest to you, sir. You really want to get this over and done with, finished with your testimony. Please try to restrict your answer to what you are being asked. Answer the question, the whole question and nothing but the question. Don't volunteer more information because that can only prolong your testimony here, and I think it's in your interest to get out of this courtroom the sooner the better. So we'll have a 25 -- or we'll have a 30-minute break starting from now. Thank you. I think the witness would like to leave the courtroom first. Thank you. 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness, we are waiting for him. Do we have much longer, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do not. I know you're glad to hear that. I was going to let you know that I am not going to question this witness any further regarding the last issue, which was whether or not there was an ABiH command that all the men go to Susnjari. Another colleague is going to cover that. I just have a few questions about ambushes and then I'm finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek? It's okay. You can start. It only makes a little bit of a noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, I would just like to ask you a few questions about the ambushes and then I'll be finished. In your statement of the 19th of July 1995, you indicated that when you reached the village of Babuljica there was an ambush and then later on when you were in the woods in a place called Kamenica, there was also an ambush; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: There was no ambush in the village of Babuljica. I don't recall saying there was an ambush. There was shelling from different weapons of the Serbs but there was no ambush there. There were wounded people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then can you just tell me approximately from the time you left Susnjari with the column, how many ambushes you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: It was such a large number of people, it could have been a hundred ambushes and it could have been none. I told you earlier how the column proceeded and what happened. What happened, I already told you. I don't know about the number of ambushes. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: The column was simply cut. The soldiers continued on and the majority of the civilians were left behind. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So then would it be a fair statement, Witness, that you cannot give us any number of ambushes you were involved in except the one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I think that it is so complicated, and if I were to talk to you for days you would never understand it. You simply don't understand the situation, the chaos that was reigning, the confusion. You will not understand even if I were to explain it to you for days. As for you asking me to tell you how many ambushes there were, I've already told you what happened. I cannot say how many there were. I don't even understand what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, Witness, I appreciate that and that's one of the reasons I was asking, but would it be a fair statement, then, that during the course of your trek with the column, that it was fairly non-stop shelling and shooting going on during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I've told you before, we came to Susnjari, which is where the main column started off from. There was a lot of shooting from Serb weapons, probably they were Serb weapons, the shooting didn't come from Mars. There were multiple rocket launchers. The fire was also coming from Serbia, from across the River Drina, from Bratunac, and they said before there were these VBRs and this is where they were shelling Srebrenica from in 1993. And people, as we were walking, were saying, "That's where the VBR is firing from." People were wounded. After the column was formed in the evening, it was quiet, there was no firing, but after the column entered the woods, then you could hear the shells, the shelling began, and then general chaos broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. And that actually, the very last sentence of your answer, once the column started into the woods, would it be a fair statement that it was non-stop shelling and shooting from the Serb army and not Mars? Really, yes or no. If you can answer that yes or no, I would appreciate it. It's last question I have.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: The question is very long. Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. I'll try. Once the column started into the woods, once you formed up and entered the woods, was the shelling and the shelling began, and general chaos broke out, did the shelling continue non-stop until you surrendered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I think that I explained but I will try to explain again. There was a large number of people, about 15.000. I don't know how many kilometres the column stretched for, perhaps ten kilometres. People were not walking right next to each other. Maybe they were five metres away from each other. So I can only talk about the section of the column that I was in. I don't know whether the beginning of the column was also shelled. I think I explained it all very clearly. When there was shelling, when it began, it went on the whole day and the night until we began to surrender, the entire day and the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Meek. Who is next? Madam Nikolic who is representing Lieutenant Nikolic will be cross-examining you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would like to put a number of questions to you. If you could help me to understand some of the events that you lived through. I would like to go back to the 11th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When the command of the B and H army issued the order to separate men from women and when it established which group would take which route. This took place on the 11th, in the evening, the 11th of July 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I can tell you that -- actually, we heard from people that there was this order or that the command of the B and H army ordered that. Nobody else could have done that, for the able-bodied men to go towards Tuzla through the woods and the civilians should go to Potocari. It wasn't anything strict. This is my answer. I really don't recall more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. So the order said that they should assemble at Susnjari and then after that to go on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Somebody ordered that, or perhaps it was the B and H army. I don't remember details. There were many people. This is my answer. I don't know any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You were not in the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: But your father was; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I'm going to tell you about that. My father was in the army, was a member of the army, formally. After Cerska and Konjevic Polje fell, I think he did belong to some unit there, I don't remember the number or anything like that. After arriving to Srebrenica, I think that he wasn't really active or anything like that. I haven't finished. I haven't finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: After coming to Srebrenica, I think that he wasn't active because I know that my father didn't go anywhere, he never had a weapon, he didn't have a uniform. So throughout 1993 and 1995, during the Serb attacks, he did not go anywhere. He was with his family the entire time. So if he was a soldier, he was with us all the time. So it was more a formal thing. I think that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your detailed answer. I would now like to ask you to explain -- now I would like to go back to the 14th of July 1995 now, when you set off in a convoy in a truck towards the location that you later recognised and identified as Petkovci. This was on the 14th of July 1995 in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You came in front of the building that you recognised today in the courtroom. You went to the first floor. You were -- you entered the classrooms in groups; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me how many people were in each group, in the classrooms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I cannot really tell you anything about the other classrooms. I can tell you about my own, when we were climbing up the stairs, as we were going in, you could hear noise from the other classrooms, the murmur of people. You could hear that there were people in there. I was put in the last or the one but last classroom as you went along the corridor. I'm not sure which one it was. So I can tell you approximately how many people there were in my classroom. I know that there were more people than in the truck. Perhaps there were 200 people but it's just an estimate. Nobody was counting.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you came to the liberated territory, the territory under the control of the B and H army, you met with officers from the 2nd Corps security service on the 20th of July 1995. They were from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I don't know if it was the 19th or the 20th. I'm not sure about the date. It was after I crossed and after I was admitted to hospital, after my wounds were dressed, after I received my injection. So it was either on the 19th or the 20th. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'm not insisting on the date. But I would just like to show you your statement so then we can look at what you said there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at e-court document and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It was too fast. The interpreter did not catch the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. It was 4D00050. There is no signature by the witness on this document, so I think that there will be no problems with the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll see it first in any case. For the time being, please no broadcast of this document until we give clearance. What's the problem? One moment, let me have a look at it first on my --

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the English version, it's on page 2, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm looking at the English version, as you can imagine. I suggest we see it in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's safer. Let's go into private session. Are we in private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And the reason is I agree with you it's not signed but there is his name there, I think, so not knowing what questions and what answers will be to be expected, I suggest that we stay in private session until we are done, until we are done with this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to ask you to look at the following sentence. It's on line 3 from the bottom of the page, when you are beginning to talk about the settlement of Petkovci where the people were taken out and detained in classrooms, in groups numbering up to about 100 people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I think that I have the wrong text. I don't really see anything, the third line.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: From the bottom up. The part that is marked in orange.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: You mean the paragraph beginning with, "On the 14th of July"?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. This is a statement you gave to the security service of the 2nd Corps of the B and H army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, sir. One moment. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's not technically correct. If you see the statement, it's a statement where they look like, for some reason, they've wrapped in two people's statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You are correct in that. Yeah. I had noticed it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As long as that's clear as part of the record, it certainly can be asked about, of course, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic, what's your comment on that? Because indeed what has been stated by Mr. McCloskey is correct. It's two statements in one.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it can be understood like that, Your Honours. But we can ask the witness whether he agrees -- if he agrees with what the security officers of the B and H army noted in this statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Well, let me just read it once again.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: What is not clear? Can you please tell me again what is not clear to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: My question is: Do you agree with what the officers, security officers of the 2nd Corps of the B and H army wrote down, based on what you stated to them on the 20th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with everything except for the mention of the name Petkovci. Probably when we crossed over or we found out from the people in the classroom that this was the settlement of Petkovci, I didn't know that we were going to Petkovci. I didn't know where Petkovci was. This is my explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So you agree that this was on the 14th of July, that it was the afternoon, that there were about 100 persons in each classroom and you were in a location that you believed to be Petkovci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Well, this is how many trucks there were. Just one moment, please. There were about five or six trailer trucks, a few buses. There were about 100 to 200 people on the trailer trucks. So there were probably in the other classrooms. This is my explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic? Yes, let's get back to open session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, Madam Nikolic for accused Nikolic has finished her cross-examination while we were in private session. It's now the turn of Mr. Stojanovic, who is appearing for accused Borovcanin to proceed with his cross-examination. And we'll stop at quarter to 2.00 as usual, Mr. Stojanovic, hoping that you will be finished by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I believe that we will.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Listening to your testimony today, you said at one point that there was a group of soldiers of the B and H army at the back of the column too. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At one point in time, the group of soldiers passed by the column, leaving the civilians behind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes, when the shelling started, when the column stopped, those people simply passed by, and we, the civilians, couldn't move ahead, so the column simply stopped. We couldn't go any further. That's the explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us whether this was on the 12th or the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: It was on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic and Witness, please slow down a little bit. You're moving too fast. The interpreters need a very short pause between question and answer, the reason being that you both speak the same language, and they have to interpret into English and French.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the name Ejub Golic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes, it does ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see that person in the column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I heard of the name in Srebrenica, and later on, after I went over, I heard that he was either a soldier or something. I heard of the person. The name does ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The group of soldiers at the rear of the column, how strong it was, how many men were there in that group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I've already explained that, not to you but to your colleague. It was not a hundred men, it was not 50 men, it was not 200 men. The number was great so I can't tell you how many there were. I don't know if there is a person alive who could tell you how many there were, especially of those who were at the rear carrying arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The ambush that you spoke about and the number of dead that you mentioned, did all that happen on the 12th or the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: This happened on the 12th of July, in the evening, and during that night, all the way up to the early morning hours of the 13th, and on the 13th we all surrendered. We spent that previous night in the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 13th, in the afternoon, you went to the asphalt road and you surrendered by a bridge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes, in the village of Kamenica we surrendered sometime in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the bridge by which you surrendered, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Before you came to the asphalt road, did you have to go across the Kravica river?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: The village of Kamenica is the village that I visited during the war. It was a Muslim village and the bridge is over a river or a stream but I don't know the name of that stream, whether it's the Kravica stream or something else. In any case, we did not cross any streams. We came from the forest, we crossed the road, and I don't know whether we crossed the bridge or not. I can't remember whether we crossed any river but I certainly do not remember that we had to get into the water and cross by tempering our feet in the water.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you instructed to follow the transmission line when you set out with the column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I don't know what transmission line are you referring to. We did not have any instruction from anybody, so I don't know what transmission line are you referring to. I can't remember any transmission line. I can only tell you that there are some transmission lines from Tuzla to Visegrad in our neck of the woods, but I don't know whether those transmission lines are anywhere near to the place through which I passed. That would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How many soldiers were there when you came to that asphalt road and when you surrendered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I believe that you've asked me that already. But I am going to tell you again. In the forest, when people decided to surrender, the column was moving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you mean to ask him how many Serb soldiers or how many Muslim soldiers? Because he's understood you to be referring to Muslim soldiers, while I understood you to be referring to Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is precisely the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not want to interrupt you and I understand what you are talking about. But my question was: How many soldiers of the VRS were there on the road where you surrendered by the bridge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But just make a short break.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I don't know how many there were. Compared to the number of us who were captured, and who surrendered there, their -- their number was insignificant in comparison with our number, and I'm referring to that particular place. I can't tell you how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If we are to use your previous statements, would it be fair to say that there were five or six of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes. There were five or six of them on the bridge, but there were more of them lined up in front of the column. But, yes, there were some four, five or six on the bridge, but the road was very close to the bridge, some ten metres away from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And how many of you surrendered there before they ordered you to start moving on the road towards Bratunac? You've already mentioned a number of 600, a thousand to 2.000. Let me put it this way: In that place, by the bridge, before you set out to Bratunac, how many of you surrendered? How many detainees were there in total?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I can tell you what I can remember. The total number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have been over that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we have been all over this. It has been asked and answered or have answered but that was, I think, exhaustively dealt with. So next area of questions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After that you were ordered to go on walking for two or three kilometres to Kravica with your hands up in the air. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes, but this applied only to those who did not carry the wounded. We had to run towards Kravica because the buses could not pass us by, and we were running in couples, holding with our arms up in the air, with three fingers up in the air and the others were carrying the wounded and we took turns carrying the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you stopped in that opening, in that meadow, an officer approached you and addressed you. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes. When we sat down in the meadow, there were a lot of us there. I was somewhere in the middle. He was standing in front of a tank and he started talking to us. I don't know whether he was an officer but he did have an appearance of an officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And he wore a bandana on his head. That's what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How did he wear this bandana, tied around his forehead?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: It was a black bandana which was tied somewhere in the back of his head, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And he told you that he was from Serbia, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes. He said that he was from Serbia and then he started delivering a speech of some sort as to what we should do, what we were supposed to do, where we would be taken, what we would get, what we wouldn't get, whether we would be exchanged or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you that you would be transported to some hangars in Bratunac and that from there you would be taken to be exchanged amongst other things?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes. He did say that amongst other things, but before that, we were there for two or three hours and we had to listen to some other slogans and shout out some slogans ourselves, like, "Long live Serbia. Long live the king." Some people were killed there. He told us that we would be taken to a hangar in Bratunac but that we wouldn't get any supper. But I'm sure that he must have known what would happen there to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please answer my questions only because we want to bring your testimony to an end. At one point, lorries arrived; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did these lorries arrive from the direction of Bratunac or did they arrive from the direction of Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: They came from the direction of Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And the person who might have been an officer, did he stop the lorries in order for you to get on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember. I didn't see that. I don't know why he would have to stop them. I believe that it was their intention to come and pick us up. They were not just passing by.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You say that you entered a special lorry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that it was the last because there was a Golf police vehicle that followed us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned that police Golf, was that a blue vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I believe that in my statement I explained it well. The Golf where we surrendered was blue. There was a civilian Golf and a police Golf and I believe that that same Golf was following the convoy. It may not have been the case. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you see anything over the sides of the lorry in which you were loaded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: The lorries were covered in tarpaulins save for the back of it through which we climbed the lorries. On that day they were covered only partially, and on the following day, they were completely covered in tarpaulins, even the back of the lorries.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How late was it when you set out towards Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but it was sometime in the afternoon, maybe five or 6.00 in the afternoon, at dusk. I believe that it was already dark when we arrived there. I don't know how long it took us to get to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the uniforms of the soldiers who were there, did you see any insignia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: There may have been insignia but I didn't see them. I was so depressed that I was not interested in a thing. We were just sitting down and I can't remember anything else. I can't remember whether there were any insignia or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what time of day it was when you passed through Kravica, when you went towards Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: There were so many people on the lorries and lorries were covered that I could not see the route that we took. They told us that we were being taken towards Bratunac but I didn't know where we were going. There were so many people. I was somewhere in the middle of the lorry and it was not possible for me to see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you spend any time in Kravica at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I can't remember. As far as I remember, we didn't. We just stopped in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Through the back of the lorry in which you were, could you see the road that you were moving on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I told you that this was the longest lorry that exists. It did not have a trailer but it was very long and I was sitting somewhere in the middle and there were so many of us that I couldn't see a thing. Save for at the moment, as I was getting on to the lorry, I saw that Golf. Later on, I didn't see it. I didn't know what route we took. When we arrived in Bratunac, I saw lights in the buildings, that's how I suppose that we had arrived in Bratunac, but that's all I can tell you. I didn't see anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You arrived in Bratunac in the evening, when the lights were already lit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes. I would say so. At that time, the lights were lit and later on I saw the lights again. We stopped in the vicinity of some buildings. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How long was the journey, in your estimate, from the moment you boarded the lorries to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I can't -- I don't know. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Stojanovic. Who is next? Mr. Krgovic is appearing here as defending General Gvero and he will be starting his cross-examination today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I'm going to ask you questions so as to enable to you answer by just yes or no. I would kindly ask you to make a short pause before answering my questions in order to allow the interpreters to interpret your words correctly and in order to avoid overlapping.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Maybe I'll have to explain things, not just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something about the events that took place on the 6th of July 1995. On the day when the attack on Srebrenica started. On the 6th of July you resided in Slapovici in the Swedish settlement; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, the attack started on the units that were close to Slapovici and also on the area of Srebrenica, and I'm referring to the BH army units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I have to say that I can't answer just by saying yes or no. From that settlement, you could see that hilltops where the UNPROFOR was and the BIH army units if there were any there. I believe that that's what I stated in my statement. And one could see the explosions and you could hear shell noise coming from the shells fired by the Serbs, and we were somewhere between those lines, between the Serbs and the UNPROFOR, and that's why we were able to both see and hear everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So BiH army units were there in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I didn't see them. I just say that they might have been there together with UNPROFOR. The UNPROFOR units were not that close but I told you the name of the hill where the UNPROFOR was and where BiH army units might have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: -- 00046. Both versions, B/C/S and English version. Exhibit 4D00046. Do you have this version in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: I can't read it. It's absolutely illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I could kindly ask the technical service to blow up the beginning of this document, if possible. I'm going to read this to you and you can try and follow.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Again, this is illegible. I can't read. Maybe you could provide me with the original hard copy. Maybe I'll be able to follow then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, we can go into private session. And we have only got two minutes left in any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in private session, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Is this the statement that you provided to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Collapse entirely the English version. We don't need it for the time being on the screen. And concentrate on the -- no, collapse it. It means -- okay. All right. Now, see if you can just work on this. Zoom in the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first paragraph and the sentence begins with, "On the 6th of July."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Which line?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me see. It's line 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of July 1995, line 8.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On July 6, 1995, the Chetniks started shelling the houses and the positions of our units.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113
utterances.text: This is what I must have heard. Maybe it wasn't them, but this is my explanation. Actually, this was a line that was set up before the UNPROFOR came. This was the separation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, is this the time for me to end today's cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not my intention to keep anyone here beyond the time limit because there is another Trial Chamber that needs to start at 2.15 and a full 30 minutes are required. We will continue tomorrow. Let's go into open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, we have to finish -- we have to stop here because another Trial Chamber will continue with another case at 2.15. So we'll continue with you tomorrow morning. In the meantime, usher, please just make sure there is nobody in the strangers' gallery or public gallery. And I think you can escort the witness out. They have left any way. So that's it. Do I take it that you will be able to conclude the cross-examinations tomorrow, Madam Fauveau and Mr. Haynes? And Mr. Krgovic of course?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So your next witness is 54, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So be prepared for 54, Witness 54 tomorrow morning. I wish you a nice afternoon and evening and see you all tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 1st day of November, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.
